parts.note: read not as the model but as work made of twigs: basketry woven from pliant shoots

explanation.surface: A famous 1960s fashion model photographed on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twiggy' looks like the model's name, but here it is an adjective: work that is twiggy is woven from twigs and osiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Basket-making material of woven osiers and twigs gives this name to the craft and its products.

parts.note: Scott's series of historical novels takes its name from the first of them, published in 1814

explanation.surface: Opening volume of a fiction series.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Walter Scott's whole series is named after its first book.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's debut novel gave its title to the entire sequence of his fiction.

parts.note: the lady's-slipper orchid suggests the glass slipper of the fairy tale

explanation.surface: A gift of flowers for the fairy-tale heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: The genus name means 'Venus's slipper', and the plant is called lady's-slipper: Cinderella is known for her slipper.
explanation.definitionFit: This botanical genus is the lady's-slipper orchid, so a slipper flower suits the girl with the glass shoe.

clue.text: I and we are objectively worried by birds on the run

indicators.note: worried here means pulled about, so these letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: objectively, as the object of a verb, I becomes me
we in the objective case becomes us

explanation.surface: A couple fret about some escaped birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'objectively' turns I and WE into their object forms ME and US; 'worried' rearranges MEUS. 'On the run' fits flightless birds, which run rather than fly.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian flightless birds that are fast runners.

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
counts are continental noblemen, equal to earls

explanation.surface: Stories told about a hundred aristocrats.
explanation.definitionFit: Narratives or reports of events are synonyms of tales.

definitions.meaning: 'the ...' or 'cratur' is an Irish nickname for whisky
anything made or created by a maker

explanation.surface: A spirit described by how it is produced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The crater' as an Irish name for whiskey is an old colloquialism.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish slang for strong drink, and a being that has been brought into existence.

clue.text: High calling involving a knock-down blow

definitions.text: High calling involving a knock-down blow

parts.words: High calling involving a knock-down blow
parts.note: a high calling sounds like a vocation, but it is a higher bid called at an auction, settled by the hammer knocking the lot down

explanation.surface: A lofty vocation that includes a crushing punch.
explanation.walkthrough: At an auction a lot is 'knocked down' with a blow of the hammer to whoever calls the highest offer.
explanation.definitionFit: Offering more than a rival at auction or in bridge.

parts.note: the shortened form of north used in wind names such as ...'-easter

explanation.surface: Someone out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short in the wind' suggests breathlessness, but it means the shortened form of a compass point in names of winds.
explanation.definitionFit: The clipped form of the compass point used in sailors' names for winds, nor'wester and nor'easter.

parts.note: Chekhov's play 'Three ...' follows three siblings

explanation.surface: A character from a Russian play.
explanation.definitionFit: Olga, Masha and Irina are the female siblings of Chekhov's play.

clue.text: Not as where an operatic bride drops an "h ' !

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Not as where an operatic bride drops an "h" ! (5)': ASTON is ASHTON (Lucia's family name in Lucia di Lammermoor) less H, and 'Not as' rearranges to ASTON, but no word defines the answer and 'Not as' has no anagram indicator, so the clue is two wordplays with no definition the grammar can hold.
annotationWithheld.clue: Not as where an operatic bride drops an "h ' !

definitions.meaning: fumes or visible exhalations, mists given off
the old phrase 'the ...' meant depression or hysteria

explanation.surface: Someone lights up whenever they feel down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when in' is just a link between the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Fumes rising from something hot are one sense; the Victorian ailment of melancholy, 'a fit of the vapours', is the other.

clue.text: Gets ten otters by unlawful means

indicators.note: something done unlawfully is crooked, so these letters are bent out of their order

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: A poacher acquires a catch of ten otters illegally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by unlawful means' looks like part of the definition, but it signals that X (ten) and OTTERS are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To wring money or goods out of someone by threats is to obtain them forcibly.

clue.text: British variety sometimes makes the disgruntled traveller do so

definitions.text: British variety sometimes makes the disgruntled traveller do so

parts.words: British variety sometimes makes the disgruntled traveller do so
parts.note: the national train network's name supplies the noun, and a fed-up passenger complaining bitterly supplies the verb of the same spelling

explanation.surface: A grumble about British train services provoking passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: British Rail was the UK's state railway; the same word as a verb means to complain angrily.
explanation.definitionFit: A track for trains and a verb meaning to rant or protest share one spelling.

clue.text: What some writers do to examine payment

parts.note: to con is to study or scrutinise, as in conning a text
a tribute was a payment made by a subject state

explanation.surface: Writers checking what they are paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link. CON in the sense 'peruse, study' is old but still a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers who supply articles to newspapers or magazines are said to write for them in this way.

clue.text: A match for old Nick at the prize-fight ?

definitions.text: A match for old Nick at the prize-fight ?

parts.words: A match for old Nick at the prize-fight ?
parts.note: the devil is called Old Scratch, and a fit boxer comes to the line scratched on the ground at the start of a bout

explanation.surface: A boxer good enough to fight the devil.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Nick and Old Scratch are both names for the devil; in bare-knuckle boxing a fighter had to come up to a line scratched in the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Fit and up to the required standard, from boxers coming to the mark to start a round.

parts.note: Odysseus's wife unpicked each night the shroud she wove by day, to delay her suitors

explanation.surface: Unravelling cloth in the manner of the ancients.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Odyssey, Odysseus's wife promised to remarry when her weaving was finished, then undid it nightly; the verb means to undo work so as to stall.
explanation.definitionFit: To unravel one's work to gain time, as the faithful wife of Ithaca did with her loom.

clue.text: Foreign student going north before noon

parts.note: élève is French for pupil or student

explanation.surface: An overseas student heads up north early in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going' is a link; 'north' looks like a reversal signal in a down clue, but this is an across and it just gives N.
explanation.definitionFit: The hour just short of midday on the clock is the one before twelve.

clue.text: It's a bit rude in the City, this lack of polish

indicators.note: the bit of rude is placed inside the word for the City

parts.note: the City is London's financial district, written CITY

indicators.note: only a part of the word rude is taken, the run of its first three letters

explanation.surface: A coarse remark heard in the Square Mile shows a want of refinement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a bit rude' reads as a remark about manners, but 'a bit' takes only part of the word. The City is the City of London, the financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarseness or roughness of manner is the absence of refinement.

clue.text: Mocking when abroad in the dance

indicators.note: the word for abroad is placed inside the dance

parts.note: a fling is a lively Scottish dance, as in the Highland fling
out means away from home, abroad

explanation.surface: Laughing at people while dancing overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' is only a link; 'abroad' looks like a setting for the scene but supplies a short word meaning away from home.
explanation.definitionFit: Treating rules or people with open contempt is a form of scorn.

clue.text: It's unskilled to be sluggish about export in short

indicators.note: the word for sluggish goes round, about, the short form of export

parts.note: inert means sluggish, slow to move
exp is the abbreviation for export

explanation.surface: Being slow to deal with exports shows a lack of skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' and 'to be' are only links; 'in short' marks an abbreviation of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking expertise means clumsy and untrained.

parts.note: Dickens's Scrooge is the type of the stingy man, so sharing his traits means being tight-fisted

explanation.surface: Someone showing a hint of Dickens's famous skinflint.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingy and grasping like a hoarder, which is Scrooge's defining trait.

parts.note: voices or instruments sounding the same note together, and so any accord

explanation.surface: A firm, solid deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like 'solid', but it means the sound of voices: singing the same pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Several voices on one pitch, and by extension acting in concert, is harmony of sound.

parts.note: the cry of West Ham fans, nicknamed the Hammers, read as the cheer of those who work with hammers

explanation.surface: A football chant for a team's supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: West Ham United, a London football club, are 'the Hammers'; metalworkers at the forge are the ones who wield hammers.
explanation.definitionFit: Metalworkers at an anvil use hammers as their chief tool.

clue.text: But nowadays it is not always a place of conventual seclusion

definitions.text: But nowadays it is not always a place of conventual seclusion

parts.words: But nowadays it is not always a place of conventual seclusion
parts.note: a monastic house now often names a grand country house or church long since without monks or nuns

explanation.surface: A remark that old religious houses have changed use.
explanation.walkthrough: Many English country houses and parish churches keep the name of the monastery they replaced, such as Woburn or Westminster.
explanation.definitionFit: Once a home for monks or nuns, the word now often names a stately home or great church.

clue.text: Not a word, man, to the elephant ; it's spell-binding

parts.note: mum means silent, as in 'mum's the word'
bo is old American slang for a fellow or mate
Jumbo was the famous elephant of London Zoo, and the name for any elephant

explanation.surface: Someone tells their companion to keep quiet near the elephant, a mesmerising sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link. 'Spell-binding' is read as binding by a spell: meaningless incantation.
explanation.definitionFit: Gibberish ritual words used as magic or to mystify are incantations meant to enchant.

parts.note: not an angry remark but the Latin word for a cross

explanation.surface: An angry remark, or perhaps a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is Latin for cross, and in English means the essential point.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for a cross, borrowed into English for the decisive heart of a problem.

parts.note: the knob an organist pulls to select pipes doubles as a word for finish

explanation.surface: Wondering about the death of a church musician.
explanation.walkthrough: An organ's draw knobs controlling ranks of pipes share their name with a halt.
explanation.definitionFit: A finish or halt, and also an organ control.

clue.text: Sailor with cash and I go for the composer

parts.note: a tar is an old word for a sailor
tin is slang for money

explanation.surface: A seaman with money sets off to find a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' and 'go for' are links. Giuseppe Tartini was an 18th-century Italian violinist and composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartini wrote the 'Devil's Trill' violin sonata, so he is a composer.

parts.note: Eve was made from a bone taken from Adam's side, and the word is a jocular term for a wife

explanation.surface: A thin married woman.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis, Eve was made from Adam's bone, so a wife is humorously called by that bone's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved chest bone, from which Eve was formed, gives an old joke name for a spouse.

clue.text: Send upstairs in a stylish manner ?

definitions.text: Send upstairs in a stylish manner

parts.words: Send upstairs in a stylish manner
parts.note: being 'sent upstairs' is promotion to the House of Lords, and the style is a title of nobility

explanation.surface: Showing a guest to the bedrooms with some elegance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kicked upstairs' or 'sent upstairs' means elevated to a peerage; 'style' here is a form of address, a title.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a person a rank or name of honour, as when someone is raised to the peerage.

parts.note: the phrase for dread is read literally: actually going down beneath water

explanation.surface: Showing the dismay of someone who has had bad news.
explanation.definitionFit: To go under the surface of water is literally to sink.

parts.note: a countdown ends in a rocket being fired skyward, and the word for that firing also means outcome

explanation.surface: What happens when the countdown reaches zero.
explanation.definitionFit: The final outcome of events, from the last shot in an archery contest.
